markdown: # Hot singles in your area: Vol1
Oct 24, 2026 [#vim](https://blog.nerdware.ca/tags/#vim)
Context:[`printf`](https://neovim.io/doc/user/helptag/?tag=printf)

You are connected to a remote server and come across a csv that contains all of the details about that ad you just saw for *Hot Singles in your Area*, you obviously open the file, but between the wrapping and the formatting you have no chance of obtaining the sweet fruit of this digital cornucopia.
![x](https://blog.nerdware.ca/img/x.png)
Close your eyes for 5 seconds, and imagine what it would be like to be in such a position.
Finished? did you really do it? did you feel that sense of despair? Well, worry not dear reader, I am here to guide you on your journey.
> hot-singles-in-your-area.csv

The first thing we are going to want to do, is give ourselves some consistent column sizing. To do that, for each of our columns we are going to get the max length, and then pad the length to that size for everything smaller than it. If not already enabled use `:set ruler` and `G` to check your row count in the bottom right (for us we have 55 rows). To get our column count we can inspect using dry-mode multi-match line replace `s/,//gn` and we find that there are 8 commas which yields 9 rows. With that knowledge in our heads, we will perform the following macro-register-magic:
> **Note:** You will need to use your thinker on whether or not each of these require a \<CR\> after
:let @c=1
go
:let @m=0
qf
v0"iy
:let @n=strchars(@i)
:let @m=max([@m,@n])
q
go
go
qx
q
go
:let @m=0
qw
@cf,l
vt,"iy
:let @n=strchars(@i)
:let @m=max([@m,@n])
q
go
@cf,l
go
qx
@cf,l
ct,<C-r>=printf('%-' .. @m .. 's', @")<CR><Esc>
@cf,l
q
go
qo
:let @c=@c+1
:let @m=0
go
go
q

Okay, well, now look at us go. We’ve got ourselves a nicely padded table, but there is a bit of a problem with our rows now because we most likely have `wrap` set… that’s an easy enough fix though for eager beavers like us `:set nowrap`.
Yeah, now this is looking *GOOD*.
One thing about tables though is that as we are scrolling down through our list, we may forget what the column headers were. Fear not, for we can use a clever little trick with the `:resize` command!
:split
:resize 1

Oooh now look at us, who needs Excel! Hop into the lower window with `<C-w>j` and start scrolling down! That’s exciting, but, oh no, wait, I scrolled back horizontally and my header did not follow us! Drats! We’re ruined! Or, by the grace of Vim, are we okay?
We’re okay.
:set scrollbind
<C-w>k
:set scrollbind
:set scrollopt=hor,jump
And just like that, when we scroll horizontally our header row now tracks us. Lovely.
Now dear reader, I hate to leave you in suspense, but you will have to tune in next time to figure out how we are going to sort and filter our new prettified list to find our perfect match
